content: In the 1950s and 1960s, perineal hyaluronidase (HAase) injections were commonly used to reduce perineal trauma, pain, and the need for episiotomy during vaginal deliveries. Reports from that time suggested that HAase administration was a simple, low-risk, cost-effective, and efficient method to decrease perineal trauma without causing adverse effects. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of perineal HAase injections in reducing spontaneous perineal trauma, episiotomy, and perineal pain during vaginal deliveries. To gather relevant data, researchers searched multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of October 31, 2013), the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), and the Networked Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations (both as of April 1, 2013). They also reviewed reference lists of retrieved studies and contacted relevant organizations. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared perineal HAase injections with either placebo injections or no intervention during vaginal deliveries. Two authors independently assessed the trials for inclusion, extracted data, and evaluated the methodological quality of the studies. The data were cross-checked for accuracy. The search identified six potentially eligible studies, of which two were excluded. Four randomized controlled trials, involving a total of 599 women (with data available for 595 women), were included in the analysis. Two trials (283 women) compared perineal HAase injections during the second stage of labor with placebo injections and were deemed to have a low risk of bias. Three trials (one of which was a three-armed trial analyzed twice) involving 373 women compared HAase injections with no intervention; however, two of these trials were at high risk of bias. Data from the four trials (599 women) suggested that perineal HAase injections during the second stage of labor were associated with a lower incidence of perineal trauma compared to the control group (average risk ratio [RR] 0.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.50 to 0.95, Tau² = 0.08, I² = 82%). However, there was no clear evidence of a reduction in the incidence of episiotomy (average RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.29, Tau² = 0.17, I² = 66%), firstand second-degree perineal lacerations (average RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.33, Tau² = 0.30, I² = 85%), or thirdand fourth-degree perineal lacerations (RR 0.12, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.13). Data from two trials (283 women) comparing HAase injections with placebo injections showed no clear evidence of a reduction in perineal trauma (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.06, Tau² = 1.07, I² = 7%), episiotomy (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.32 to 1.89, Tau² = 0.27, I² = 54%), firstand second-degree perineal lacerations (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.40, Tau² = 1.11, I² = 10%), or thirdand fourth-degree perineal lacerations (RR 0.12, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.13). Data from three trials (373 women) comparing HAase injections with no intervention suggested a lower incidence of perineal trauma (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.88, Tau² = 0.08, I² = 78%). However, there was no clear evidence of a reduction in the incidence of episiotomy (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.42, Tau² = 0.16, I² = 70%) or firstand second-degree perineal lacerations (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.10, Tau² = 0.18, I² = 59%). No side effects were reported in any of the included trials. Additionally, none of the trials reported on perineal pain or other pre-specified secondary outcomes, such as perineal trauma requiring suturing, blood loss, dyspareunia, urinary incontinence, fecal incontinence, assisted delivery rates, women's satisfaction, Apgar scores below seven at five minutes, or the need for admission to a special care baby unit. The authors concluded that perineal HAase injections during the second stage of labor were associated with a lower incidence of perineal trauma compared to control or no intervention. However, there was no clear evidence of benefit when compared to placebo injections. The observed reduction in perineal trauma in non-placebo-controlled comparisons may be influenced by bias and confounding factors, and these findings should be interpreted with caution. The potential role of perineal HAase injections in reducing perineal trauma remains uncertain due to the lack of an established optimal dose, absence of follow-up data, and the limited number of high-quality trials and reported outcomes. Further rigorous randomized controlled trials are needed to determine the effectiveness and safety of perineal HAase injections in vaginal deliveries.
